target.thesis: Force is fixed by a public status-conferring practice of adoption and uptake, not by producer psychology. This is supported by divergence tests against objectives-based proxy views, with Moffatt compatible with it but not established as a case of illocution.
target.headline: Both the literalist and the relocating camps grant that a speech act's force is fixed by the psychology of some producer, whether the model or its principal. Cases in which a chatbot's output was held to bind a deployer with no content-specific intention show that force can be fixed by the normative practice of adoption and reliance, with no producer-side intention at all.
target.target: Proxy accounts (Green & Michel, Arora) and, shared with them, the denials by Gubelmann and Skiba: the assumption that illocutionary force requires a content-specific producer-side intention or objective.
target.sketch: Take Moffatt v. Air Canada, where a tribunal held the airline to its chatbot's statement of a bereavement-fare policy. No designer or deployer had any objective regarding that content, so Green and Michel's Armstrong-style 'objectives' condition for proxy speech acts fails. The tribunal also did not treat the utterance as fiction or as mere signalling, so Mallory's fictionalism misdescribes the practice. The objective theory of contract and of representation gives the general pattern: an utterance counts as a promise or assertion by an agent because of the agent's role, the uptake, and the allocation of risk, whatever the agent intended. The key premise is that this is a case of illocution and not merely of liability. The evidence is that the standard felicity vocabulary applies: the statement is 'a misrepresentation', 'a promise', and so on. If that holds, the question 'who is the author of the model's speech act?' is badly posed. Authorship is conferred by the practice and not discovered in the producer's mind. The result is a non-psychological, deontic-status view that proxy accounts approximate only by accident.

findings.part: Named target: Green & Michel's Armstrong-style 'objectives' condition for proxy speech acts
findings.source: Green & Michel, "What Might Machines Mean?", Minds and Machines 32, 2022
findings.what_they_say: They replace speaker-meaning intentions with Armstrong-style objectives, so that non-conscious systems can illocute. They propose that artificial speakers typically act as proxies performing speech acts on behalf of their human creators.
findings.note: The target is described accurately, so the thesis does not misattribute the view. Whether Moffatt defeats the objectives condition is the thesis's own argument, and I did not find anyone making it.

findings.source: Arora, "Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions", Philosophy & Technology 37, 2024
findings.what_they_say: Arora argues against 'functionalist' views of machine assertion. He defends a refined proxy view on which responsibility lies with designers or deployers, and only utterances meeting certain epistemic-responsibility or epistemic-state conditions on those humans count. A later paper reports that Arora insists genuine assertion requires a conscious principal who can be held accountable.
findings.note: Arora's condition is a producer-side epistemic one, which fits the thesis's target. It is framed as epistemic responsibility, not as a content-specific objective, so the thesis must say how Moffatt fails that condition and not only Green & Michel's.

findings.part: Named targets: the claim that Gubelmann and Skiba share the 'content-specific producer-side intention or objective' assumption
findings.source: Gubelmann, "Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now)", Philosophy & Technology 37, 2024; Skiba, "Artificial Speech Acts" (PhilPapers abstract)
findings.what_they_say: Gubelmann argues that to illocute a being must have intentions and that LLMs have none, so they are no speakers. Skiba's abstract describes a norm-based argument against LLM assertion, generalised to all speech acts. Neither abstract says a designer or deployer needs a content-specific intention or objective.
findings.note: Gubelmann's premise concerns the LLM's own intentions. Skiba's argument is norm-based, which is not an intention requirement. Lumping them in with the proxy accounts looks like a misdescription. I checked abstracts and excerpts only, not the full papers.

findings.part: Core claim: force is fixed by public conversational roles and normative effects, not by speaker psychology; proxy views as an analogy for responsibility practices
findings.source: "Who asserts when no one asserts? Functionalism, proxy responsibility, and conversational ideals in the age of LLMs", Synthese, 2026
findings.what_they_say: The abstract names two strategies. Functionalist accounts characterise assertion by the public conversational roles and normative effects of utterances, not by the speaker's psychological states. Proxy views trace accountability back to human agents. It says the proxy strategy works as an analogy that captures existing practices of responsibility attribution, and it asks whether the two can be paired.
findings.note: This is the most recent synthesis I found. It already maps the non-psychological functionalist option and the idea that proxy talk approximates a responsibility practice. I saw only the abstract and excerpts.

findings.part: 'Who is the author of the model's speech act?' is badly posed
findings.source: "Assertion, Accountability, and Large Language Models", Philosophy & Technology, 2026
findings.what_they_say: It says the intermediate positions (AI-testimony, proto-assertion, proxy assertion) typically keep some asserter or speaker-like role at some level of analysis. It then has a section on a pragmatic, accountability-based approach. Proxy views are described as anchoring assertion's normative expectations in agents other than the source of the output.
findings.note: The critique that proxy views still need a speaker role, and the accountability alternative, sit close to the 'authorship is conferred, not discovered' claim. I saw only fragments, so how far it goes is unverified.

findings.part: Non-psychological, behavioural criterion for LLM speech acts
findings.source: "Communicative Action in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Theorizing LLMs as Communicative and Strategic Agents", Philosophy & Technology, 2026
findings.what_they_say: The authors propose non-intentional, 'behavioral' illocutionary acts that are not tied to a cognitive-volitional complex, and they offer a behavioural criterion for them. They still concede that LLMs fail Searle's sincerity condition and so cannot perform genuine illocutionary acts.
findings.note: It decouples some force from producer psychology, but by behavioural indistinguishability and not by a public status-conferring practice.

findings.part: Rejection of both proxy accounts and Mallory's fictionalism
findings.source: Williams & Bayne, "Chatting with bots: AI, speech acts, and the edge of assertion", Inquiry, 2024
findings.what_they_say: They consider the proxy-assertion response and the fictionalist response to the chatbot-assertion dilemma and argue that neither is satisfactory. They propose 'proto-assertion' instead. They also note that Green & Michel's account only grounds chatbot assertion where the chatbot is deployed to generate text on behalf of a person or organisation who has adopted a blanket attitude.
findings.note: A referee will cite this as prior dual rejection and prior scope criticism of the proxy view. The positive view differs from a public-status account.

findings.what_they_say: Mallory argues that engagement with chatbots is prop-oriented make-believe. On his view the outputs are literally meaningless but fictionally meaningful, and they give quasi-testimony.
findings.note: Mallory holds the view the thesis ascribes to him. The thesis's objection (the tribunal did not treat the output as fiction) is a legal-practice datum, not a philosophical refutation.

findings.part: Key premise: Moffatt is a case of illocution and not merely of liability
findings.source: Tribunal decision as reported in McCarthy Tétrault, "Moffatt v. Air Canada: A Misrepresentation by an AI Chatbot", 2024; St-Hilaire, UBC Law Review case comment
findings.what_they_say: The tribunal found Air Canada liable in negligent misrepresentation, a duty-of-care and reasonable-care analysis. It rejected the argument that the chatbot was a separate legal entity. Commentators read the decision as reaffirming that organisations answer for their systems' misrepresentations to the public, whoever or whatever produced them.
findings.note: The legal framing is duty of care and responsibility for website content. I found no promise or illocutionary vocabulary in the tribunal's own reasoning, only in press coverage. The evidence for illocution is therefore thinner than the thesis assumes.

findings.part: Key premise: Moffatt shows illocution, not liability
findings.source: "Speech Acts and Large Language Models" (PhilArchive preprint)
findings.what_they_say: The paper treats the Air Canada ruling as a prime example of an utterance going straight from the locutionary to the perlocutionary level. It argues that chatbots lack the intention needed for genuine illocutionary acts.
findings.note: A published reading of this very case that explicitly skips illocution. It is a rival interpretation of the case and not an argument against the thesis's general claim.

findings.part: Objective theory of contract and representation as the general pattern; role, uptake and risk allocation over intention
findings.source: Gervais & Nay, "The Phantom Agent: Artificial Intentionality and Legal Responsibility", Stanford, 2026
findings.what_they_say: They argue that existing principles of objective assent, electronic agency and apparent authority go a long way toward resolving cases where mindless AI systems generate legally consequential conduct. Intention is treated as a normative tool for gating legal effect, allocating blame and managing risk.
findings.note: This is a legal-scholarship evidence base for the objective-theory pattern. It concerns attribution and liability, not illocutionary force, so it does not close the liability-versus-illocution gap.

findings.part: Uptake and allocation of risk as the practice that attributes a chatbot's statements
findings.source: Oliver, "Contracting by Artificial Intelligence", 2021; practitioner analysis "Can Chatbot Interactions Lead To Enforceable Contracts?"
findings.what_they_say: Australian authority is cited for the objective theory: contract depends on intentions conveyed by words and actions, not actual subjective intent. The practitioner piece says whether a chatbot binds its company depends on whether customers reasonably understand it to be the company's authorised instrumentality, which is analogous to apparent authority.
findings.note: Doctrinal support for the pattern. It also shows the same pattern is well worked out in law for chatbots.

findings.part: Empirical uptake: ordinary people allocate responsibility for chatbot statements to the deploying company
findings.source: YouGov, "Consumers hold companies responsible for AI chatbot errors", 2024; "Blame the Bot: Extending Attribution Dynamics in Chatbot-Consumer-Brand Interactions", J. Current Issues & Research in Advertising
findings.what_they_say: In a survey of over 18,000 consumers, 54% put primary responsibility on the company using the chatbot and 26% on its developer. A two-study experiment found that consumers track responsibility through ownership chains, blaming the brand or provider when they own the chatbot.
findings.note: These studies show where blame goes, not what force the utterance has, so they support the allocation-of-risk half only.

findings.source: "Artificial Speech and Its Authors" (ResearchGate; author not identified in my results)
findings.what_they_say: The visible fragments summarise Green & Michel as holding that language generators can at best perform proxy speech acts on behalf of their developers. They also say that scholars use 'proxy assertion' to mark that such output stands in for acts carried out by the humans who built the models.
findings.note: A paper on the authorship question that the thesis calls badly posed. I saw only citation fragments, so I cannot say whether it argues the thesis's position.

findings.part: Conversational-role versus speaker-tied conceptions of assertion
findings.what_they_say: It divides theorists into those who tie assertion to the speaker and those who tie it to the conversational role of the utterance. It adds that proxy status need not exclude artificial illocutionary standing.
findings.note: It confirms that the role-based versus speaker-based split is already standard, so the thesis cannot present it as new. The page was a snippet only.

finding.what_is_left: Moffatt-type cases, where a deployer is held to a chatbot's statement though no designer or deployer had any objective regarding that content, put pressure on the sufficiency of Green & Michel's objectives condition. They also put pressure on Arora's producer-side responsibility condition. A role-and-uptake account of which party is answerable fits them, in the way the objective theory of contract and apparent authority already do. Whether the tribunal's finding of negligent misrepresentation shows that the statement had assertoric or promissory force, and not just that its deployer bears the risk, is not settled by the case. The functionalist and accountability literature has already put the general view that force is public-role and normative-effect based, so the thesis's contribution is limited to the Moffatt-based divergence argument against the objectives condition. Gubelmann and Skiba should probably be treated as a separate target, since their arguments turn on the LLM's lack of intention and on norms, not on a producer-side objective.
finding.not_found: I found no source that uses Moffatt as a divergence test against the objectives condition for proxy speech acts, and none that argues the tribunal's reasoning shows illocution and not just liability. I found no direct engagement with Searle's status functions, Brandom's deontic scorekeeping, or Ludwig's work on authorised spokespersons beyond a passing citation of Ludwig. I did not retrieve Butlin & Viebahn's 'AI Assertion', Rosen & Dale's 'LLMs Don't Do Things with Words', or the full text of any 2026 paper listed above. The 2026 pieces may anticipate more than their abstracts show. The empirical search found only consumer-blame and attribution studies. I found no psychology, linguistics or experimental-pragmatics work on whether ordinary speakers treat chatbot outputs as promises or assertions (force), so that gap is untested, not clean. Most of the philosophy is behind paywalls and I read abstracts and excerpts, so the silence is weak evidence.

sep.why: The theses are about what fixes illocutionary force (a public, status-conferring practice versus producer intention), which is the speech-acts debate; social-ontology covers the deontic-status and conferral view of authorship; and contract-law covers the objective theory of contract and Moffatt-style liability.

findings.position: Force conventionalism: force is fixed by a public, conventional procedure with a conventional effect, not by the speaker's psychology.
findings.who: Austin; Searle (weaker form); Reimer (illocutionary conventions); Millikan (natural conventions)
findings.quote: There must exist an accepted conventional procedure having a certain conventional effect, that procedure to include the uttering of certain words by certain persons in certain circumstances…
findings.note: The 'public status-conferring practice' half of the thesis is the standard Austin/Searle conventionalist line.

findings.position: Uptake as a condition on performing a speech act: an act can misfire without audience uptake, and a systematic lack of uptake can silence a speaker.
findings.quote: Other attempts at speech acts might misfire because their addressee fails to respond with an appropriate uptake: I cannot bet you $100 on who will win the election unless you accept that bet.
findings.note: The 'adoption and uptake' component is already in the entry through Austin and the silencing literature.

findings.position: Intentionalism: force is fixed by manifest communicative intention (Strawson) and by overt commitment (Green), so producer psychology matters. The entry also argues that mere conventions are not required.
findings.quote: What makes an utterance of a sentence in the indicative mood a prediction rather than a command, for instance, is that it manifests an intention to be so taken
findings.note: The entry endorses the opposing intentionalist view that the thesis rejects. It also says conventional procedures are not necessary for every act.

findings.position: Uptake is not required for some speech acts, such as refusing, inviting and surrendering.
findings.quote: Bird (2002) denies that the speech act of refusal requires uptake. Such an illocution is, he contends, like inviting and surrendering, which can occur whether or not their intended audiences grasp or accept the proffered illocutions.
findings.note: Challenges uptake as a general determinant of force.

findings.position: Force is individuated by publicly accessible commitment and norms, such as the 'How do you know?' challenge. The entry stresses that commitments are not undertaken merely by intending them. Public norms of assertion and conjecture can ground divergence tests.
findings.quote: speech acts involve intentional undertaking of a publicly accessible commitment; further, that commitment is not undertaken simply by virtue of my intending to undertake it, even when it is common knowledge that this is what I am trying to do.
findings.note: This gives the thesis a public-norm basis, though the entry still makes intention a necessary part.

findings.position: Davidson's autonomy of linguistic meaning and the claim that no device can guarantee force. This would be a referee's challenge to any practice-fixed view of force.
findings.quote: there could be a society with a convention that utterance of a certain expression constituted performance of a certain illocutionary act, even those utterances that occur on stage or as used by jokers or storytellers
findings.note: The Hare/Green exchange shows what a convention-based view must answer about simulated or intention-lacking uses.

findings.position: Characteristic aims (perlocutions) as individuating speech act types. This is the nearest thing in the entry to an 'objectives-based' view.
findings.who: Austin; T. Cohen 1973; Searle and Vanderveken
findings.quote: A type of speech act can have a characteristic aim without each speech act of that type being issued with that aim
findings.note: The nearest analogue to the 'objectives-based proxy' targeted by the thesis, though the entry does not call it a proxy.

nearest_positions: Force conventionalism — Austin, Searle (weaker form), Reimer, Millikan
Intentionalism / overt commitment — Strawson 1964, Green, Grice
Uptake-dependence of illocution and silencing — Austin, Langton/Hornsby, with Bird and Maitra dissenting
per_thesis.entry_silent_on: The entry does not discuss 'Moffatt' or any case of that kind. It has no 'divergence tests' against 'objectives-based proxy' views, and it does not discuss non-human or institutional producers of utterances (e.g. AI outputs) as candidate illocutions. It does not use the phrase 'status-conferring practice of adoption'.

findings.position: Conferralism: a social status is held because of other people's attitudes or dispositions in a context, not because of the bearer's or the producer's own states. This is the closest existing version of 'status fixed by uptake'.
findings.quote: A social property is “conferred” on an object, according to Ásta, if the object has the property because of some attitudes of people. A baseball umpire, for instance, confers the property of being a strike on certain pitches.
findings.note: Status-by-uptake is already a named view. Ásta's conferral rests on community attitudes or dispositions rather than on a practice, which is the one point where the thesis differs.

findings.position: Searle's status-function theory: status is imposed by collective acceptance or recognition, through Declarations. The status does not depend on the speaker's private psychology alone.
findings.quote: What imposes these statuses is collective attitudes: our collective acceptance or recognition that they have those statuses.
findings.note: A public adoption-and-uptake account of force is largely a Searlean move. The thesis must say how it differs by making the practice, not the attitudes, do the work.

findings.position: Performatives and the linguistic construction of the social: utterances establish facts merely by being uttered, and speech acts can be constitutive of social identities.
findings.quote: Certain utterances are “performative”: merely in uttering them, we establish facts in the world.
findings.note: This gives the thesis its performative, public-act framing. The entry does not mention illocutionary force or uptake by name.

findings.position: Mentalistic and individualist accounts of how social categories are set up place the construction work in the participants' mental states. Bratman derives shared intention from individual attitudes. Searle's institutional facts depend on mental states 'not on practices'.
findings.quote: he does not require that rules be implemented in behavior: institutional facts depend only on mental states in a society, not on practices.
findings.note: These are the views the 'not producer psychology' clause opposes. The entry also records that practice-based replacements often slide back into mentalism (Bourdieu's habitus).

findings.position: Heterogeneity of anchors: social categories are not set up by one uniform kind of practice, and practice theories lack the resources to accommodate that diversity.
findings.quote: Even theories of practice, he argues, do not have the resources to accommodate this heterogeneity.
findings.note: This challenges a single public practice of adoption and uptake as what fixes force.

findings.position: Practice theories are hard to read ontologically, and it is often unclear whether they make a constitutive claim or merely tell a causal narrative. That is exactly what a referee would press against 'fixed by a practice'.
findings.quote: it is hard to tease apart different kinds of ontological claims they make, and also hard even to know when these theories are making an ontological claim, as opposed merely to telling a narrative of causal influence.
findings.note: The thesis must say whether practice constitutes force or only causes it. The entry's causal/ontological distinction (2.3) applies here.

findings.position: Whether anchoring is synchronic or diachronic. Uptake that comes after an utterance raises the question of whether history can be constitutive.
findings.who: Epstein 2015 and Schaffer 2019 (for diachronic determination); Bernstein 2016 (against); Searle (synchronic)
findings.quote: Diachronic ontological determination is a matter of controversy: in favor see Epstein 2015, Schaffer 2019; opposed see Bernstein 2016
findings.note: Adoption and uptake unfold over time, so the thesis must take a side.

findings.position: Some debates are dismissed as merely verbal. A divergence test between rival accounts of force could be read as terminological.
findings.who: McGrath 2008; Chalmers 2011; Barnes 2014; Díaz-León 2022 (against the dismissal)
findings.quote: merely because a debate is verbal does not exclude it from being metaphysically substantive.
findings.note: This is a weak neighbour, relevant only to the 'divergence tests' methodology.

nearest_positions: Searle's status functions, imposed by collective acceptance and declaration — Searle 1995, 2010
Conferralism, where status depends on others' attitudes or dispositions in context — Ásta
Performativity and speech-act constitution of the social — Austin, Butler, Thomasson
Practice theories as the basis for setting up categories (with the worry that they collapse into mentalism) — Bourdieu, Giddens, Schatzki
per_thesis.entry_silent_on: The entry does not discuss illocutionary force as such, Austinian uptake, 'objectives-based proxy' views, or anything called 'Moffatt', nor divergence tests of this kind. It does not discuss the force of legal or institutional texts. Section 5.7 (Law) and the rest of the entry are cut off in the provided text, so any treatment of force in law cannot be checked.

findings.position: The objective theory of contracts. Legal effect is fixed by the public, objective meaning of the parties' speech acts, not by what they privately intended. This is the nearest existing version of 'not producer psychology'.
findings.who: Hotchkiss v. National City Bank (court); proponents of the 'objective theory of contracts'; R2 §§24, 201
findings.quote: A contract has, strictly speaking, nothing to do with the personal, or individual, intent of the parties. … If … it were proved by twenty bishops that either party … intended something else than the usual meaning which the law imposes upon them, he would still be held
findings.note: The anti-psychologism is already doctrine. The thesis must show its practice-based account differs from the objective-meaning view.

findings.position: Contract law imposes obligations regardless of the promisor's attempt to disclaim promissory force. This is a divergence case where public rules, not producer attitude, settle force.
findings.who: Lucy v. Zehmer; the 'not a legally enforceable agreement' clause cases; Scanlon's 'I'm not promising' disclaimer discussion
findings.quote: Contractual obligations are imposed notwithstanding a promisor's attempt to negate their promissory intent
findings.note: These are ready-made divergence cases. They are framed as problems for the harm-based and economic views, not as tests of illocutionary force.

findings.position: Rosen's Gricean reframing keeps intention central. What matters is the parties' 'legal intentions' to produce legal effects through their speech acts. The legal-intention view is itself a producer-psychology view of force.
findings.quote: The parties' legal intentions—which seem to matter, ultimately—can come apart from their semantic intentions.
findings.note: A referee will cite this as the main intentionalist rival. The thesis must argue that legal intention is not what fixes force.

findings.position: Raz's promising and the standard picture ground obligation in an intention to bind by the very act of communicating. The entry says the standard picture needs an account of prospective intention.
findings.quote: a promise arises when a person communicates … an intention to undertake by the very act of communication an obligation to perform an action
findings.note: The intention-based analysis of promissory force is the default the thesis opposes.

findings.position: The standard-form clicking puzzle. The law finds contractual intent in thoughtless acts where intentionality seems absent, which supports force being conferred publicly rather than by psychology. The entry's own fix is a dispositional theory of intention, which is the closest psychologistic rival.
findings.who: Rakoff 1983; Radin 2007, 2014; Barnett 2002; the entry's dispositional proposal
findings.quote: the consumer's actions in virtue of which the law finds an intention to be bound appear thoughtless—that is, lacking in intentionality.
findings.note: This is the best divergence evidence. Nobody in the entry draws the status-conferral conclusion from it.

findings.position: The 'reasonable person' gloss on objective meaning works as an objective proxy for intention. It is the closest thing to an 'objectives-based proxy view' in the entry.
findings.who: R2 §201 and the objective theory's proponents
findings.quote: objective meaning concerns what a reasonable person in the position of the addressee would have inferred was meant based on the available evidence.
findings.note: A divergence test against this proxy would turn on whether uptake or addressee inference does the work.

findings.position: Offer and acceptance are defined in terms of manifestations and of justifying the addressee's understanding. This is a public-uptake structure, and it also fixes offer and acceptance as legal powers conferred by rules.
findings.who: Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§24, 50; Markovits and Benson on the contract relation
findings.quote: so made as to justify another person in understanding that his assent to that bargain is invited and will conclude it.
findings.note: Offers a doctrinal hook for an 'adoption and uptake' account. The entry does not give it a speech-act reading.

nearest_positions: Objective theory of contracts: public or reasonable-person meaning, not private intent — Hotchkiss, R2 §§24, 201
Rosen's Gricean legal-intention framework: force turns on parties' legal intentions, distinct from semantic intentions — Rosen (2011), following Grice
Intention-based promise and standard-picture views, with the dispositional-intention repair for form contracts — Raz, Fried, the entry's §2.3, Radin, Barnett
per_thesis.entry_silent_on: The entry never discusses illocutionary force, Austin or Searle, or 'uptake' as a speech-act concept, nor a status-conferring or institutional-practice account of force. Grice is its only speech-act resource. It never mentions Moffatt, so it neither supports nor undermines Moffatt as a case of illocution. It does not discuss 'objectives-based proxy views' by name, and it offers no divergence-test methodology for separating practice-fixed force from intention-fixed force.

theses: Force is fixed by a public status-conferring practice of adoption and uptake, not by producer psychology. This is supported by divergence tests against objectives-based proxy views, with Moffatt compatible with it but not established as a case of illocution.
